justification_text:
My point estimates reflected a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a recent market price around the $265–$266 range. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing level, expecting very little net movement given typical daily volatility in equity index ETFs like SPY. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the forecast slightly higher to around $267–$268, reflecting a mild bullish bias consistent with the long-run positive drift of equity markets, while acknowledging that a week is still too short a window for that drift to be meaningful relative to noise. At the one-month horizon, I carried that drift further to roughly $270, which corresponds to an annualized return in the low-to-mid single digits — a reasonable central expectation for a broad equity index under normal conditions.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to historical volatility patterns for the S&P 500. SPY typically exhibits daily volatility of around 1–1.5%, which compounds over longer horizons. For one day, I applied a fairly tight band of roughly plus or minus $6–7, reflecting that short-term price movements are mean-reverting in distribution even if not in direction. Over one week, the band widened to roughly plus or minus $12–13, and over one month it expanded further to plus or minus $25, consistent with a square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty. Macroeconomic data releases, Federal Reserve communications, and earnings reports all contribute to realized volatility in ways that standard historical volatility estimates may understate during stressed periods.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in inflation data prompting a hawkish Fed pivot, a geopolitical shock, a credit event in financial markets, or a sharp earnings disappointment from large-cap technology companies could easily produce a 5–10% drawdown within a month, breaching the lower bound of my interval. On the upside, a surprisingly strong labor or inflation print that signals imminent rate cuts, a major positive geopolitical resolution, or a powerful short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above my upper bound.

Finally, my intervals assume something close to a normal, stationary volatility regime. If volatility itself were to spike — as it does during VIX shock events or liquidity crises — the actual distribution of outcomes becomes fat-tailed and my stated 90% confidence intervals would be too narrow. Structural breaks, such as a sudden change in Fed policy framework or a systemic financial event, represent the tail risks most likely to render my probabilistic forecast poorly calibrated at any horizon beyond a day or two.
